Chapter 10
Sample Management
In process industries such as chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and food, com-
panies that integrate sample management into their business processes
reap the greater business benefits of comprehensive information, data
visibility, and traceability by putting the necessary quality controls in
place.
Manufacturers in general and process manufacturers in particular often require exten-
sive visibility and traceability of every important material procured, produced, or
received through a stock transport order (interplant transfer). The system’s standard
options are limited when there is a need to have separated yet categorized physical
samples that the quality inspectors and other laboratory personnel can record results
of and use to make usage decisions. Sample management provides a comprehensive
and in-depth solution to physical samples of various sources (externally procured, pro-
duced in house, customer or supplier complaints, etc.). With sample management, the
system supports the following types of sample generation:
 Automatic generation of physical samples during inspection lot creation
 Manual generation of physical samples—if needed, with reference to an inspection
lot or other reference objects
 Manual and multiple generation of inspection lots for existing physical samples
 Sample data records
For each physical sample, the system creates a physical-sample record, which contains
the following essential information:
 Sample number
 Sample type (from goods receipt, from procurement or production, from customer
complaints, from stability study)
 Physical sample category (primary sample, pooled sample, reserve sample)
 Sample origin (material, batch, order)
In this chapter, we’ll explain the necessary plant settings that need to be in place. Then
you’ll learn how to set up a sample-drawing procedure, which is an important master
data step in sample management, followed by the checklist for quality management
(QM) master data that you need to ensure is already in place. Then, the chapter moves

10 Sample Management
476
on to goods receipt from the procurement process and how the system automatically
creates planned physical samples of various sample categories. Next, we move on to
how sample management integrates with production processes, especially for in-
process or during-production inspection. The chapter ends with the configuration
basics of sample management.
10.1 Plant Settings
In this step, you make the necessary configuration settings that act as a control for
business users to enter information on the number of containers at the time of goods
receipt for a purchase, process, or production order. You also incorporate the sampling
procedure that the system refers to if it’s unable to find the required information in the
master data setup for sample management. This is necessary for the system to calcu-
late the sample size on inspection lot creation for sample management by using the
sampling procedure.
For the relevant plant-wise settings for sample management, follow menu path SAP
IMG  Quality Management  Basic Settings  Maintain Settings at Plant Level. Choose
the relevant plant, which in this example is plant 1710 (see Figure 10.1). In the Insp. Lot
Creation tab, choose Recording of number of containers required in Enter Container at
GR. This setting doesn’t let the business user save the goods receipt for a purchase or
process order until information about the number of containers is entered. Further, in
the Settings for Sampling Procedures area, enter the code for a previously created sam-
pling procedure, “PFIX5”, in the Sample Management field. This sampling procedure
denotes that the system will create a fixed sample size of five units upon goods receipt.
Figure 10.1 Plant Parameters
© 

477
10.2 Master Data
Note
Refer to Chapter 3 for how to create a sampling procedure that you can use in this step.
While creating a sampling procedure, choose the Sample Management radio button
that’s available in the Inspection Point area.
10.2 Master Data
As with other business processes into which QM integrates, sample management also
requires that you maintain the master data before you can run the business processes.
Apart from the regular master data, such as relevant inspection type activations in the
material master and creating inspection plans, you also need to maintain a sample-
drawing procedure and assign it to the material’s inspection plan for planned physical
samples.
In the following section, we’ll discuss master data specific to sample management,
including the sample-drawing procedure, inspection plan, and ensuring the QM master
data checklist is adhered to.
10.2.1 Sample-Drawing Procedure
You can use the sample-drawing procedure to plan automatic (planned) physical sam-
ple generation during inspection lot creation. In a sample-drawing procedure, you
define how many samples the system should draw, whether the business user needs to
confirm a sample’s drawing, and which category of physical sample to draw. The fol-
lowing physical sample categories are available for selection:
 Primary sample
You draw the primary sample directly from a material/batch stock. You can inspect
these samples or create pooled samples from them.
 Pooled sample
You create this sample by mixing other physical samples from the same material/
batch.
 Reserve sample
You draw the reserve sample from a material/batch stock and store it for other
inspections.
With the sample-drawing procedure, you can also control when the system should
automatically print out the sample-drawing instructions, which contain detailed infor-
mation on how to draw a sample. If the material is supplied in different physical sample
containers, you can store corresponding drawing instructions depending on the phys-
ical sample container. For all planned physical sample creation, you assign the sample-
drawing procedure to the material’s inspection plan, master recipe, or routing.

10 Sample Management
478
In sample management, it’s often also necessary to draw physical samples that weren’t
originally planned and are therefore known as unplanned physical samples. This busi-
ness scenario generally applies when you have to conduct additional tests on a mate-
rial that didn’t show satisfactory inspection results and for which you need more
physical samples to conduct another round of testing. For such unplanned physical
samples, the following two options are available:
 You can manually generate an entirely new physical sample.
 You can manually generate a physical sample for an existing physical sample record.
In the sample-drawing procedure, you can determine whether the system automati-
cally or manually releases (or confirms) the automatically created physical samples.
When you confirm a physical sample drawing, the system releases some or all corre-
sponding physical samples. Considering the compliance aspects of Good Manufactur-
ing Practice (GMP), there may be a need for quality inspection to manually confirm
physical sample drawing. Further, there is the option to enter digital signatures (see
Chapter 3), which ensures that only authorized employees can execute certain activi-
ties (e.g., the confirmation). You have to manually confirm the manually created phys-
ical samples.
To make the relevant settings for the sample-drawing procedure, use Transaction QPV2
or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data 
Sample  Sample-Drawing Procedure  Edit.
Note
To display the sample-drawing procedure, use Transaction QPV3 or menu path Logis-
tics  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Basic Data  Sample  Sample-Drawing
Procedure  Display.
Figure 10.2 shows the initial screen for the sample-drawing procedure. For this exam-
ple, enter “S200” and select the Consider No. of Containers checkbox so that the system
makes it mandatory for a business user to enter the container information in the
inspection lot. In addition, and only if required, select the Confirmation Req. checkbox
to enable the business user to confirm sample drawing as a separate step.
Figure 10.2 Sample-Drawing Procedure
© 

479
10.2 Master Data
Tips and Tricks
If a sample-drawing procedure is no longer in use or becomes obsolete, you can block
its usage by selecting the Blocking indicator checkbox.
Choose sample-drawing procedure S200, and then choose Sample-drawing item on the
left side; this leads to the screen in Figure 10.3.
Figure 10.3 Primary, Pooled, and Reserve Samples
Figure 10.3 1 shows the Primary samples tab, where you enter the unit of measure for
Lot Container as “EA” (each). From Sample contnr (container), you can choose the rele-
vant container that you’ll use for storing physical samples from the dropdown. In Size
factor, you enter a number that the system then uses to multiply with the physical
sample quantity. For example, if you enter a size factor of 2, then the system creates a
physical sample quantity double the originally calculated value. In the Number of Sam-
ples area, you can define how the system calculates the quantity of physical samples.
Here, apart from the option to have a fixed number of (primary) physical samples, you
can use a sampling scheme that the system can use to calculate the number of physical
samples. If you do use the sample scheme option, you also have to assign the Insp.
severity, as well as the acceptable quality level (AQL value).
Finally, you can also enter a formula to calculate the number of physical samples. For
this example, enter the fixed number of physical samples as 3, and the system auto-
matically creates three primary physical samples. Choose the Pooled samples tab 2.

10 Sample Management
480
The options for pooled samples are the same as for primary samples. Enter “2” to auto-
matically create two pooled samples during inspection lot creation. Finally, choose the
Reserve samples tab 3. Here, the system only offers the option to enter a fixed number
of reserve samples, the quantity for each sample, and the unit of measure to go with the
quantity. Enter the details shown so that the system creates one reserve sample of 3 KG.
To summarize the physical sample settings that you’ve made so far, the system creates
four physical samples—one primary sample, two pooled samples, and one reserve
sample—during inspection lot creation. We’ll show these happening when we cover
the business processes of sample management. Save your settings.
10.2.2 Inspection Plan
Figure 10.4 shows the header details of the inspection plan for material QM003 for
plant 1710, with group 50171002 (this number will appear after you save the inspection
plan) and group counter 1. The inspection plan’s Usage is set to “5” (Goods Receipt),
while its Overall Status is set to “4” (Released). It’s important to assign Insp. Points as
“200”, which is specifically available for physical samples. Here, you assign the previ-
ously configured sample-drawing procedure, S200.
Figure 10.4 Inspection Plan with Sample-Drawing Procedure
© 

481
10.3 Business Processes
Choose Operations in the screen in Figure 10.4, and it leads to the operations view of
the inspection plan. Scroll down and be sure to choose either option 2-Valuation or 3-
Automatic valuation based on insp. (inspection) point definition for the Insp.point-
Completion field. These two options enable the system to either allow manual valua-
tion by the quality inspector or trigger automatic valuation on inspection completion.
Next, choose Inspection Characteristics in Figure 10.4 (not shown but located at the top
menu bar), and the screen in Figure 10.5 appears. Here, you enter the relevant master
inspection characteristic and also assign the previously created sampling procedure PFIX5.
Figure 10.5 Sampling Procedure in Inspection Plan
Because this example covers the procurement process (inspection type 01), you need to
ensure that the following QM master data exists in the system.
10.2.3 QM Master Data Checklist
The following is the QM master data checklist:
 Inspection type 01 is active in the Quality Management view for material QM003. In
addition, activate inspection type 15 for sample management.
 Inspection plan usage 5 (for goods receipt), inspection plan usage 9 (material check),
and both inspection plans must have status 4 (released). For inspection type 15 (sam-
ple management), the system uses the inspection plan with usage 9.
Note
You can integrate sample management with inspection types 01, 02, 04, 05, and 08.
10.3 Business Processes
When materials are delivered, they’re usually in one or more containers, from which
the quality inspector draws physical samples. The system determines the scope of the
physical sample drawing from the information in the inspection plan and the assigned

10 Sample Management
482
sample-drawing procedure and prints it out on the sample-drawing instruction when it
creates an inspection lot.
Here, you perform goods receipt for an already created purchase order, in which the
system asks for information about the number of containers. It also creates a goods
receipt inspection lot, as well as physical samples of various sample categories. Then,
you release the physical samples, followed by printing labels. You perform results
recording of not only the goods receipt inspection lot but also inspection lots created
for physical samples. Figure 10.6 illustrates this process.
Figure 10.6 Business Process of Sample Management in Goods Receipt from Procurement
Process
In the following sections, we’ll show how to create a goods receipt of an already created
purchase order. The goods receipt process will prompt the user to enter details of phys-
ical samples. At the same time, the goods receipt will also create an inspection lot with
multiple physical samples. Samples are released so that standard QM processes such as
results recording and usage decision can occur. We’ll also discuss how to manually cre-
ate a physical sample.
Note
Refer to Chapter 4 to learn more about business processes in procurement and inven-
tory management, including how to create a purchase order and then perform a goods
receipt for the same purchase order.
10.3.1 Goods Receipt for Purchase Order
The supplier delivers the material that is ordered against purchase order number
4500001821, and the warehouse supervisor records the goods receipt. Access Transac-
tion MIGO or follow menu path Logistics  Materials Management  Inventory Manage-
ment  Goods Movement  Goods Movement. Select Goods Receipt and then Purchase
Order from the dropdown lists at the top.
Enter purchase order number “4500001821”. The movement type for goods receipt
against a purchase order is 101 and is shown at the top-right corner of the screen. If it’s a
batch-managed material, then the system will create a batch number and receives the
stock as quality inspection stock. When trying to save entries, the system brings up an
error message to ask the business user to enter container details (i.e., the number of

Use Transaction QA02 to view the details of inspection lot 10000000662. Choose the
Inspection Specifications tab, and the screen in Figure 10.8 appears. The system assigns
sample drawing procedure S200 to inspection lot 10000000662.

484
In the Sample tab shown in Figure 10.9, notice that the system lists the number of con-
tainers (No. Containers) as 5 EA, which you entered at the time of goods receipt for the
purchase order. The system calculates the Sample Size as 10 PC and creates correspond-
ing physical samples.
Figure 10.9 Physical Samples for Goods Receipt
10.3.3 Physical Samples for Goods Receipt
Click the Samples button shown in Figure 10.9, and the system opens a popup window
showing an overview of various physical samples created for this specific inspection
lot, as shown in Figure 10.10.
Figure 10.10 Physical Samples Overview
© 

485
10.3 Business Processes
Figure 10.10 shows that the system created four physical samples, starting with phys-
ical sample 100000008 and ending with 100000011. The system also assigns the
sample-drawing number (SampDraw) 3 to all four physical samples. This sample
drawing is a common reference point for all physical samples. There are three cate-
gories of physical samples, and these are set per sample-drawing procedure S200
that you maintained in Figure 10.3.
For details of each physical sample category, place the cursor in the Cat field and either
use the dropdown option that appears or press (F4). This is shown in the lower half of
the screen, where 1 denotes Primary Sample, 2 Pooled Sample, and 3 Reserve Sample. A
primary sample is the main sample used the sample management process. A pooled
sample can be used for multiple trials and stability studies, while a reserved sample is
used in case there’s an issue with the primary or the pooled sample, and the quality
inspector needs another sample, which can be drawn from the reserved samples. So,
the system creates one primary sample, two pooled samples, and one reserve sample,
consistent with the settings made in Figure 10.3.
The initial status of physical samples is CRTD (created), and you need to release or con-
firm a sample drawing in a separate step. All of these actions are the direct result of set-
tings made in Figure 10.2.
10.3.4 Release and Print Physical Sample Label
A physical sample with status CRTD (created) doesn’t allow subsequent business func-
tions, like creating an inspection lot of inspection type 15, without which you can’t
record results or make its usage decision. For an automatically or manually created
physical sample, you release the physical sample drawing so that it attains the REL
(released) status. To do so, use Transaction QPR2 (Change Physical Sample).
On the initial screen, enter the physical sample, and press (Enter). Choose Release
Sample from the top menu bar and save.
For automatically created (planned) physical samples, you can print out labels for phys-
ical samples. You can create these labels according to your requirements; print details
such as name, date, time, batch, sample number, and inspection lot number; and even
add a barcode. You can also manually trigger label printing for the sample data record.
To view the print labels request or send it to the printer spool, use Transaction SP02 or
menu path More  System  Own Spool Requests (see Figure 10.11).
Figure 10.11 Label Print of a Physical Sample

10 Sample Management
486
Note
Ensure that function module QPRP_LABEL_PRINT_MULTIPLE_1 is assigned to the sample
type for label printing. Refer to Section 10.5.2, where the relevant configuration settings
are discussed.
10.3.5 Inspection Lots for Physical Samples
Upon releasing physical samples and confirming their withdrawal, you can create
inspection lots of physical samples for subsequent results recording and usage deci-
sion. To create inspection lots for physical samples, use Transaction QPR5 or menu
path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Sample Management  Phys-
ical Sample-Drawing  Create Inspection Lots.
Figure 10.12 shows the initial screen to create inspection lots for physical samples and
to view the status of physical samples and their storage deadlines with Monitor Con-
trol. Enter Sample-Drawing Number “3”, and in the Monitor Control dropdown, choose
Inspection lot creation. Finally choose Execute (not shown) so that the screen in Figure
10.13 appears.
Figure 10.12 Inspection Lot for Physical Samples
© 

487
10.3 Business Processes
Figure 10.13 brings up the same four physical samples of sample drawing 3. In this step,
you specifically create inspection lots for physical samples. To do so, choose Select All
(or choose a sample) to select all four physical samples, and then choose Create Inspec-
tion Lot. In the screen that appears, refer to the Current Insp. Lot column, which con-
tains details of individual inspection lots that the system creates for all four physical
samples at the time of goods receipt, which in this example is inspection lot
10000000662. For this example, sample 100000012 was selected followed by choos-
ing Inspection Lot Creation from the top menu bar, which led to the physical sample’s
inspection lot creation for sample management 150000000004.
Figure 10.13 Worklist for Inspection Lots Creation for Physical Samples
When you save, you’ll see the log that appears upon successful (or unsuccessful) cre-
ation of inspection lots. If inspection lot creation for a physical sample is unsuccessful,
the system displays the complete reason for it (e.g., missing master data or incorrect/
incomplete inspection plans).
Tips and Tricks
You can use this same option to create multiple inspection lots for the same physical
sample. For example, after finding the initial results of the physical sample unsatisfac-
tory, say you want to retest the physical sample. You’ll need another inspection lot for
the same physical sample, need to record new results, and need to make another usage
decision.
We’ll now individually review both inspection types. The first inspection type is for
goods receipt for a purchase order (inspection type 01) and how the system prompts
the business user to select from pooled physical samples as inspection points during
the quality inspection process. The second inspection type, 15, is for the physical sam-
ple.
Note
You can also create inspection type 15 for pooled samples so that you can inde-
pendently perform all the QM functions, such as results recording and usage decision

10 Sample Management
488
for pooled samples, first, and then enter the findings as inspection points (basically
pooled physical samples) in goods receipt inspection for the purchase order (inspection
type 01).
We suggest that although the system offers several options to record results and make
usage decisions for pooled physical samples, you should evaluate all available options
to maintain a balance between having information in the system and having to enter
the inspection data multiple times.
10.3.6 Result Recording for Physical Sample: Inspection Type 15
Figure 10.14 shows Inspection Lot 150000000004 of Inspection Type 15 (Transaction
QA03), which the system creates on a physical sample of Material QM003 and the phys-
ical sample 100000012. The inspection lot consists of relevant details such as the mate-
rial document that the system created upon goods receipt for the purchase order. This
inspection type isn’t stock-based, so the remaining quality steps are results recording
and usage decision.
Figure 10.14 Inspection Lot for Physical Sample: Inspection Type 15
10.3.7 Results Recording for Pooled Samples (Goods Receipt Inspection)
The business process of results recording for the physical sample is no different from
that of inspection lot results recording. One or several physical samples can exist for an
inspection lot. You also have the option of making a usage decision for an inspection
lot only when you’ve processed and evaluated all physical samples for an inspection
© 

489
10.3 Business Processes
lot. For unplanned (manually created) physical samples, you may need to manually
release the physical samples before you can record results.
Access the screen in Figure 10.15 through Transaction QE01, and enter Inspection Lot
“10000000662” and Operation “0010” to bring up the list of physical samples avail-
able. In the Inspection point area, place the cursor on Sample, and use the dropdown
option or press (F4). Out of the four physical samples that the system creates, it brings
up only two pooled physical samples, 100000009 and 100000010, for you to choose
from as inspection points. These two available pooled physical samples as inspection
points are shown on the right side of Figure 10.15. Choose the first physical sample
(100000009), and press (Enter), which brings up the results recording screen for
inspection lot 10000000662, operation 0010, and physical sample 100000009. The
sample size is 5 PC. You record the results of these two physical samples with reference
to their inspection point and also make their usage decisions.
Figure 10.15 Results Recording of Pooled Samples: Initial Screen
Next, let’s evaluate the inspection lots for a physical sample (sample management)—
that is, the inspection lot of inspection type 15.
10.3.8 Manually Creating a Physical Sample
You can manually create physical samples at any given point in time with or without
reference to any of the previously created objects, such as material documents or sam-
ple-drawing instructions. The system offers several options to create physical samples

10 Sample Management
490
to meet business scenarios, such as physical samples of competitor goods, samples for
complaints against a supplier, or customer and physical samples for a stability study
(see Chapter 15).
When you choose one of the reference objects to create a physical sample, the system
brings up the option to enter details of that reference object so that it can logically con-
nect the newly created physical sample with that reference object. For example, if you
create a physical sample for a stability study, the system opens a popup in which you
can enter a reference of a stability study for which you want to create the physical sam-
ple. Similarly, if you want to create a physical sample for complaints against the sup-
plier, then the system opens a popup for you to enter the material document number
against which you initially received the supplier’s goods.
To create a physical sample, use Transaction QPR1 or menu path Logistics  Quality
Management  Quality Inspection  Sample Management  Physical Sample  Create.
Figure 10.16 shows the initial screen to create a physical sample.
Figure 10.16 Creating the Physical Sample: Initial Screen
The system offers various options to create different types of physical samples, which
are available when you choose the Sample Type dropdown. You can also use the copy
model function to copy data from an existing object to the next physical sample. For
example, you can use a reference of an already created physical sample to create a new
physical sample, thus saving you time and effort in data entry. Similarly, you can refer-
ence the already created physical sample drawing to attach to the physical sample.
© 

491
10.3 Business Processes
For this example, choose Sample Type 01 Goods Receipt Sample, and, in the Sample
Drawing area, select the Extend Existing radio button. Enter the previously created
physical sample Drawing Number “3” (this is the same physical sample drawing that
previously created four physical samples for goods receipt against the purchase order).
Finally, choose Sample (not shown, but located at the bottom-right corner of the
screen). This opens the popup that informs you of the details against which the system
will create the physical sample and of which it will also automatically incorporate all
the references, such as material, batch, and material document numbers.
Choose Continue to see the screen in Figure 10.17, which depicts physical sample
100000012. The system automatically references all information from physical sample
drawing 3. Notice that the status of the physical sample is CRTD (created).
Figure 10.17 Unplanned Physical Sample Creation
You can also print labels on this screen. You can enter additional information in the
fields that are available for data entry. Because this is a manually created physical sam-
ple, the system denotes this with the checkmark in the Sample manually created check-
box.
Choose the Sample Detail tab. Here, choose the sample category, such as Initial Sample,
Pooled Sample, or Reserve Sample, from the dropdown list, and enter the sample quan-
tity, such as 1 PC in this example, to denote the sample quantity of the physical sample.

492
Choose the Inspection Lot Data tab, and the screen in Figure 10.18 appears showing the
reference data of Inspection Lot 10000000662, to which this physical sample
100000019 will attach itself. Before you save your entries, release the physical sample
from the top menu bar of Figure 10.17.
Figure 10.18 Inspection Lot Data of Previous Goods Receipt Samples
Figure 10.19 shows the physical Sample Storage tab, which shows the storage location
and sample location of the reserve sample.
Figure 10.19 Physical Sample Storage
Access the screen in Figure 10.20 through Transaction QA02 for inspection lot
10000000662, and then, in the Sample tab, choose Physical Samples Overview (not
shown). Physical sample drawing 3 now extends to incorporate the new physical sample
© 

493
10.4 Physical Sample Drawing with Reference: Production Processes
100000012. The remaining steps for the manually created (unplanned) physical sample
are the same, such as creating its inspection lot, recording results, and making a usage
decision, as we previously covered for automatic creation of physical samples.
Tips and Tricks
Because you created and released the physical sample manually, you can also use Trans-
action QPR2 (Change Physical Sample) to directly create an inspection lot for the sample.
Figure 10.20 Manually Created Physical Sample as Part of Sample Drawing 4
10.4 Physical Sample Drawing with Reference: Production Processes
The business processes for goods receipt for a process or production order aren’t any dif-
ferent from those for goods receipt from the procurement process. However, in the pro-
duction process, an important business process is the in-process or during-production
process for which you want to carry out quality inspection using sample management.
Sample management integrates with all production types, such as discrete, process, and
repetitive manufacturing (REM). A typical production process involves processing a
material that goes through various operations and phases during the production pro-
cess. During the course of its production, the material attains different physical and
chemical attributes and requires physical inspections.
There are two options to handle quality inspection in production processes using sam-
ple management. The first option is that for planned physical sample drawings, you

10 Sample Management
494
can assign the sample-drawing procedure to the routing or master recipe, and the sys-
tem creates a physical sample when it creates the inspection lot. The second option is
to manually draw the physical sample on different criteria, such as drawing a physical
sample after every five hours or after every 100 PC of production. In such cases, you
don’t plan the drawing of physical samples in a sample-drawing procedure. You create
the samples manually with reference to an inspection lot or order.
In this section, we’ll show how creating a process order creates an in-process (during
production) inspection lot, which you then use as a reference to create physical sam-
ples.
10.4.1 Process Order
To create a process order, use Transaction COR1 or follow menu path Logistics  Produc-
tion – Process  Process Order  Process Order  Create  With Material. On the screen that
appears, enter Material “FG129”, Plant “1710”, and order Type “YBM1”, and then press
(Enter).
This leads to the process order header screen. Enter the Total Qty. (process order quan-
tity) of 100 PC. With production planning (PP)-relevant settings in place, the system
performs several functions, such as automatically entering start and end dates of pro-
duction. Choose the Assignment tab shown in Figure 10.21, and the system creates an
in-process inspection (inspection type 03) lot number 30000000554. Depending on
the PP settings, the system creates the in-process inspection lot either at the time of
creating a process order or on its release.
Figure 10.21 Process Order
© 

495
10.4 Physical Sample Drawing with Reference: Production Processes
You use this inspection lot number as a reference to ensure the physical sample draw-
ing. Save the process order, and the system creates a process order number that you
can note down—in this example, process order number 1002144.
10.4.2 Physical Sample Drawing with Reference
To create a physical sample with reference to a production order, process order, or mate-
rial/plant/production version combination (REM), use Transaction QPR6 or follow
menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Sample Management 
Physical Sample-Drawing  Create with Reference. Figure 10.22 shows the initial screen
to create a new physical sample with reference to production, the process order, the in-
process inspection lot, or REM’s material, plant, and production version combination.
Enter the number of physical samples that you want to create. By selecting the Simulate
Sample Creation checkbox, you simulate whether the system can indeed create the
physical samples or whether it will lead to any warnings or errors. If there’s a warning or
error message, you can first correct it before proceeding to create physical samples. In
the Detailed Data for the Sample area, you can choose a sample category from the drop-
down list and enter the sample quantity, together with the physical sample unit of mea-
sure. In the Data for Storage area (not shown but located further down the same screen),
you can enter further information about the physical samples, such as the storage loca-
tion and sample location for the physical samples that you want to create, and the sys-
tem automatically incorporates the information for all physical samples.
Figure 10.22 Physical Sample Drawing with Reference: Initial Screen

10 Sample Management
496
Tips and Tricks
It’s recommended to use the Simulate Sample Creation functionality to first simulate
and see if the system will be able to successfully create the physical samples. If not,
then this functionality will inform you of the missing or incomplete data or other set-

10.5 Configuration Basics
Configuration in sample management requires using some of the already created con-
figuration objects, such as status profile or number ranges, and assigning them. Other
configuration activities involve creating or changing configuration objects to meet
business needs. We’ll discuss these activities in the following sections.
10.5.1 Physical Sample Type Assignment to Inspection Type

during automatic (planned) physical samples creation, the system is able to find the

10.5.2 Define Physical Sample Types
To manage physical samples, you can add new sample types for necessary inspection
types. Typically, sample types that the system delivers are sufficient to meet most busi-
ness needs. If you want to use your own number range for any of the sample types, you
need to define it for the fiscal years you want.

Tips and Tricks
If you don’t want to restrict number ranges of physical samples to a predefined num-
ber of fiscal years, you can enter “9999” in the Year field to denote infinite use of the
assigned number range to the physical sample. On the other hand, if you assign year
2023 to a number range, then the system will require you to enter a new number range
when the year 2024 begins.
To define a new physical sample type, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage-
ment  Quality Inspection  Sample Management  Define Physical Sample Types. In the
Change View “Definition of sample types” overview screen, choose Sample Type 02
(Sample from production). You can assign a previously defined or standard number
range available in the system. You can maintain the Status Profile if there’s a business
need to control different functions of the physical sample through the status profile.
The standard function module is available for sample label printing, which you can use
along with the checkbox to initiate immediate printing (see Figure 10.25). Be sure to
maintain the function module for label printing as shown so that the system is able to
print labels.

10.5.3 Define Physical Sample Container
The physical sample container is the unique identification of different containers that
you use to carry physical samples. These physical sample containers can be, for exam-
ple, beakers, flasks, test tubes, or jars. You can create new physical sample containers

Choose New Entries, and enter the PSCt (physical sample container) code, together with
its description. Save your entries.
10.5.4 Define Physical Sample Locations
Physical sample locations uniquely identify different locations used to keep the physi-
cal samples. These can be various sections or divisions of the quality control. You can
create new, plant-specific physical sample storage locations (physical or virtual) with
menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Sample Management 
Define Physical Sample Locations. In the Determine Work Area: Entry popup that
appears, enter Plant “1710”, choose New Entries, and enter the storage location code and
its description. Save your entries.
10.6 Summary
This chapter covered the master data that you need to set up for sample management.
Then, it delved into business processes for goods receipt in procurement and how it
triggers physical sample creation. The business processes for sample management for
goods receipt from procurement are no different from those for goods receipt from a
production order or stock transport order. While leveraging automatic (planned) phys-
ical sample creation, you can also manually create the same (unplanned) samples as
required to meet business needs. Similarly, you can create inspection lots for physical
samples, either in a mass transaction or individually.
